Verses 138-154

(7:138) We carried the Children of Israel across the sea, whereat they came upon a people cleaving to certain idols that they had. They said, “O Moses, make for us a god like they have gods.” He said, “You are indeed an ignorant lot.

(7:139) What they are [engaged] in is indeed bound to perish, and what they have been doing shall come to naught.”

(7:140) He said, “Shall I find you a god other than Allah, while He has graced you over all the nations?”

(7:141) And when We delivered you from Pharaoh’s clan who inflicted on you a terrible torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women, and there was a great test in that from your Lord.

(7:142) And We made an appointment with Moses for thirty nights, and completed them with ten [more]; thus the tryst of his Lord was completed in forty nights. And Moses said to Aaron, his brother, “Be my successor among my people, and set things right and do not follow the way of the agents of corruption.”

(7:143) When Moses arrived at Our tryst and his Lord spoke to him, he said, “My Lord, show [Yourself] to me, that I may look at You!”

He said, “You shall never see Me. But look at the mountain: if it abides in its place, then you will see Me.” So when his Lord disclosed Himself to the mountain, He crumbled it, and Moses fell

down swooning. And when he recovered, he said, “Immaculate are You! I turn to You in penitence, and I am the first of the believers.”

(7:144) He said, “O Moses, I have chosen you over the people with My messages and My speech. So take what I give you, and be among the grateful.”

(7:145) And We wrote for him in the Tablets from all things some advice and some elaboration of all things, [and We said], “So hold on to them with power, and bid your people to hold on to the best of [what is in] them. Soon I shall show you the abode of the transgressors.

(7:146) Soon I shall turn away from My signs those who are unjustly proud in the earth, and [even] though they should see every sign, they will not believe in it, and if they see the way of rectitude they will not take it as [their] way, and if they see the way of error they will take it as [their] way. That is because they deny Our signs and are oblivious to them.”

(7:147) Those who deny Our signs and the encounter of the Hereafter, their works have failed. Shall they be requited except for what they used to do?

(7:148) The people of Moses took up in his absence a calf [cast] from their ornaments—a body that gave out a lowing sound. Did they not regard that it did not speak to them, nor did it guide them to any way? They took it up [for worship] and they were wrongdoers.

(7:149) But when they became remorseful and realized they had gone astray, they said, “Should our Lord have no mercy on us, and forgive us, we will be surely among the losers.”

(7:150) And when Moses returned to his people, angry and indignant, he said, “Evil have you substituted me in my absence! Did you lose patience with your Lord’s decree?” He threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, pulling him towards himself.

He said, “Son of my mother, indeed this people thought me to be weak, and they were about to kill me. So do not let the enemies gloat over me, and do not take me with the wrongdoing lot.”

(7:151) He said, “My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the most merciful of the merciful.

(7:152) Indeed those who took up the calf [for worship] shall be overtaken by their Lord’s wrath and abasement in the life of the

world.” Thus do We requite the fabricators [of lies].

(7:153) Yet [to] those who commit misdeeds but repent after that and believe—indeed, after that, your Lord shall surely be AllForgiving, Ever-Merciful.

(7:154) And when Moses’ indignation abated, he picked up the Tablets whose inscriptions contained guidance and mercy for those who are in awe of their Lord.

Introduction

These verses discuss the stories of the Children of Israel after they were delivered from their bondage under Pharaoh’s clan. The verses pursue the overall theme of the chapter up to here, which is the idea that whenever the religious call was made to a nation, they were to be found closer

to disbelief than belief, and the majority of them broke God’s covenant. Hence, God would bless the believers with His special grace, and would penalize the disbelievers with His excruciating punishment.

These verses cover the following parts of their story:

(1) The Children of Israel were given passage across the sea.

(2) They asked Moses to make an idol for them to worship.

(3) They worshiped the calf when Moses had gone to the tryst of his Lord.

(4) The Torah was revealed to Moses.

Commentary

(7:138) We carried the Children of Israel across the sea, whereat they came upon a people cleaving (yaʿkufūna, from ʿukūf) to certain idols that they had. They said, “O Moses, make for us a god like they have gods.” He said, “You are indeed an ignorant lot.”

According to al-Mufradāt of al-Rāghib, ʿukūfiis “to turn to something and adhere to it out of reverence.”

… make for us a god like they have gods…: The implied meaning of this comparison is: “Make for us a god like they have gods made for them” [where the last part is omitted].

The Children of Israel followed the religion of their ancestor Abraham. Some of their previous prophets were Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, all of whom propagated monotheism. Their religion subscribed to God as the sole deity to be worshiped, and believed Him to be transcendent, incorporeal, and free from having physical properties like shape and size. Nevertheless, the Israelites had materialistic and empiricist inclinations, and lived on the basis of sense perceptions, as we can infer from their stories. They did not pay any attention to what lies beyond sensory perceptions, except for some formalities, but not as a genuine or authentic belief. Moreover, they lived for several years under the rule of Egyptians who were idol-worshipers. That impressed itself on their souls, even though their racial pride maintained their ancestral religion for them to some extent.

Most of them viewed God as a physical being among other physical beings. That was their impression of God. We can even observe this in the extant Torah today, which presents us with a very anthropomorphic view of the divine essence. W henever Moses tried to describe the transcendent nature of the Truth to them in a way that their minds could grasp,

they would divert it to shapes and figures that were fabrications of their imagination. For this reason, when they saw in their way a community that subscribed to their idols, they desired to have the like of that for themselves. They asked Moses to make for them a god, just like the gods that they have and adhere to.

Moses found no alternative to describing God’s oneness to them other than lowering the discussion to the level of their limited understanding. First he blamed them for their ignorance about the status of their Lord, for it should have been clear to them that the way of the idol-worshipers is wrong and fruitless. Second, he “defined” God for them through

describing His attributes. This is how he clarified that their Lord cannot be represented by an idol or defined by an image. We shall see this below.

(7:139) “What they are [engaged] in is indeed bound to perish (mutabbar), and what they have been doing shall come to naught.”

Mutabbar is derived from tabār, which means halāk (destruction, death, perishing). The verse literally says, “W hat they are in,” which means the path and tradition that they pursue, which was idol-worship. What they have been doingrefers to their ritual practices. The meaning is: The path of these idol-worshipers is doomed to damnation, and their religious deeds are void. Therefore, it is not befitting of an intelligent person

to incline toward it. Instead, one should serve God, which leads one to eternal happiness and permanent good.

(7:140) He said, “Shall I find you (abghīkum) a god other than Allah, while He has graced you over all the nations?”

Abghīkum means “to seek, to procure.” Here Moses introduces and describes their Lord to them.

… Shall I find you a god other than Allah…: What he means is: “Any god that I might make or assign for you would be other than Allah, but the One that you must worship is Allah, for He is your Lord.” Moses effectively refers to God’s Lordship by describing Him as: He has graced you over all the nations. Their conversation can be reconstructed and elaborated as follows:

The Israelites: Make for us a god like they have gods (7:138).

Moses: How can I procure for you a manufactured lord, for that would be other than your real Lord: Allah. The worship of any other lord would be void and doomed to perish.

The Israelites: How can we worship Him when we do not see Him, and have no way of seeing Him? (This is one of the principal arguments of idol-worshipers.)

Moses: Worship Him based on what you know of His attributes.

He is the One Who has preferred you over all nations through His manifest signs, His true religion, and His deliverance of you from Pharaoh and his misdeeds.

As we can see, this verse presents a lofty truth to weak intellects through subtle expressions and concise arguments.

(7:141) And when We delivered you from Pharaoh’s clan who inflicted on you (yasūmūnakum) a terrible torment, slaughtering (yuqattilūna, from taqtīl) your sons and sparing (yastaḥyūna, from istiḥyāʾ) your women, and there was a great test in that (dhālikum) from your Lord. The verb sāma yasūmu means “imposing something on someone in a humiliating and disgraceful way.” Taqtīl means “killing abundantly.”1 We saw the word istiḥyāʾ before [in verse 7:127]. It means sparing their women and letting them live in order to serve them as maids. The demonstrative pronoun dhālikum (that) apparently refers to the above mentioned tortures of Pharaoh’s clan against the Children of Israel.

Some exegetes have suggested that the verse is addressed to the Jews who were living at the time of the revelation of the Qur’an. God reminds them of the great favor that He showed their forefathers at the time of Pharaoh. However, it is more consistent with the context and flow of the verses to say that the verse is addressed to the very companions of Moses who lived at his time. It is addressed to them as an expression of surprise, for they so quickly forgot God’s great blessing upon them, whereby He rescued them from such a dreadful calamity. We shall see another similar expression of surprise—albeit in the third person—below, where God says: Did they not regard that it did not speak to them, nor did it guide them to any way? (7:148).

1

(7:142) And We made an appointment with Moses for thirty nights,

1 In other words, the verbal pattern tafʿīl in this case implies abundance and multitude. (Trans.)

and completed them with ten [more]; thus the tryst (mīqāt) of his Lord was completed in forty nights. And Moses said to Aaron, his brother, “Be my successor among my people, and set things right and do not follow the way of the agents of corruption.”

Mīqāt is close in meaning to waqt (time). Majmaʿ al-bayān says:

The difference between mīqāt and waqt is that mīqāt is a specific time that is assigned for some activity, but waqt is the general time and duration of something. That is why the word mīqāt is used for the hajj. Mawāqīt al-ḥajj [extracted from verse 2:189] are the places that are assigned for the pilgrims to enter the state of iḥrām.

The verse describes God’s appointment with Moses in two stages: it was initially set for thirty nights, then that was extended by another ten nights. The verse then concludes that they added up to forty. Elsewhere we read: And when We made an appointment with Moses for forty nights

(2:51), where the verse only refers to the subtotal of both appointments. In other words, the verse in Sūrah al-Baqarah [2:51] states that the entire forty nights were appointed, and the verse in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf [7:142] clarifies that the total mentioned in the other verse consisted of two appointments. The meaning is: God gave Moses an appointment of thirty nights to draw him near to Himself and speak to him. Then He gave him another appointment of ten nights as a complement to the initial appointment. Thus the tryst of his Lord was completed in forty nights.

The verse mentions “nights” instead of “days” even though Moses also spent the days of that period on Mount Ṭūr. Besides, it is more common to use days when referring to the appointed times of activities. In this case, however, night is more pertinent, because the tryst was to draw closer to God, indulge in His remembrance, and engage in private conversation with Him. The night is more suitable for this purpose because that

is when the senses are less distracted, and the soul is more prepared for intimacy. One of the blessings of this nocturnal tryst was the revelation of the Torah. The same idea can be found in these verses: O you wrapped up in your mantle! Stand vigil through the night, except a little… Indeed soon We shall cast on you a weighty word.Indeed the watch of the night is firmer in tread and more upright in respect to speech,for indeed during the day you have drawn-out engagements (73:1-7).

… And Moses said to Aaron, his brother, “Be my successor among my people…”: Moses said this when he was departing them for his tryst. We can infer this from the phrase, Be my successor among my people, because succession only makes sense in the absence of the original person. The Children of Israel are called my people and his people in several places in this chapter. Their ascription to Moses is in harmony with the other similar stories in this chapter, where Prophets Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ and others called their people: O my people.1 Otherwise, they are referred to as the Children of Israel in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā.

… and set things right and do not follow the way of the agents of corruption”: Moses commanded his brother to set things right, and to not

follow the path of those who make mischief. Aaron was a divine prophet and an infallible messenger. He would never sin, nor follow the chiefs of corruption in religious matters. Moses knew his this better than anyone. Therefore, what is meant here cannot be a prohibition against religious disbelief and disobedience. Instead, it pertains to governmental and managerial affairs. Moses advised his brother to not follow the counsel and

approval of the corrupt individuals among his people throughout the term of his succession, when Moses is absent. We can infer this from the phrase, and set things right, which shows that the next part of his advice—and do not follow the way of the agents of corruption—is about conducting their social affairs properly. He should not govern them according to the way of the agents of corruption. He should not make decisions based on what they advise him as the appropriate thing to do.

This statement shows that there were a group of rebels and troublemakers among Moses’ people who used to cause mischief, sabotage his

plans, and anticipate calamities to betide him. That is why Moses warned his brother against following their way, lest they may disturb his affairs, and conjure plots against him. While Moses had suffered all those troubles and tribulations to establish order and unity among them, these people wanted to disunite the Children of Israel and throw them into disarray.

1 See verses 59, 61, 65, 67, 73, 79, 85, 93, and the author’s exposition of them in

volume 15 of the English translation. (Trans.)

(7:143) When Moses arrived at Our tryst and his Lord spoke to him, he said, “My Lord, show [Yourself] to me, that I may look at You!” He said, “You shall never see Me. But look at the mountain: if it abides in its place, then you will see Me.” So when his Lord disclosed (tajallá, from tajallī) Himself to the mountain, He crumbled it (dakkan), and Moses fell down (kharra, from khurūr) swooning (ṣaʿiqan, from ṣaʿqah). And when he recovered (afāqa, from ifāqah), he said, “Immaculate are You! I turn to You in penitence, and I am the first of the believers.”

Tajallī (manifestation, epiphany) is “to take on jalāʾ (appearance, expression, disclosure).” Dakk means “pounding something, hitting something hard.” What is meant by dakk (pounding, crushing) in this verse is

madkūk (pounded, crushed, levelled).1Khurūr means “to fall, to collapse.” There are two meanings for ṣaʿqah: (1) dying; (2) fainting, losing consciousness and sensory perception. Ifāqah means regaining consciousness and

sensory perception. After fainting, when the person recovers their state of sound consciousness and balanced intelligence, it is said that “the person afāqa from their swoon.” Based on its apparent structure, the verse can be interpreted as follows:

When Moses arrived at Our tryst…:That was the tryst that We appointed for him.

… and his Lord spoke to him…: God spoke His words to Moses.

… he said…: Moses said.

… “My Lord, show [Yourself] to me (arinī), that I may look at You (anẓur ilayka)”…: Moses asked God to show Himself to him, so that he may look at Him. There are three stages here in sequence:

(1) First one must be given the ability, the means and the establishments (called tamkīn or tamakkun) to look at something.

(2) Then one can look at it (called naẓar) in order to see it.

(3) Then one would see it (called ruʾyah).2

1 In other words, the maṣdar (gerund, verbal noun) here implies the meaning of mafʿūl (passive participial noun, accusative case). (Trans.)

2 The first stage is what is meant by: arinī (show to me). The second stage is indicated by anẓur ilayka (that I may look at You). The last stage is not explicitly mentioned in the verse, as it is implied by the rest of the verse, Therefore, what he meant was: Enable me to look at you (anẓuru ilayka), so that by looking at you I may see you (arāka).1 … He said…: God said to Moses.

… “You shall never (lan) see Me…”: The negational particle lan here implies “never.”

… But look at the mountain (al-jabal)…: The definite article al- in al-jabal (“the” in the mountain) shows that there was a mountain right there before Moses.

… if it abides in its place, then you will see Me”…: You can not bear to see Me. Instead, look at the mountain. I will manifest Myself to it; if it stays where it is and can endure My vision, then you would know that you too are capable of looking at Me and seeing Me.

… So when his Lord disclosed Himself…: When God manifested.

… to the mountain, He crumbled it…: Through His appearance and manifestation, God demolished the mountain into small pieces and particles in the air, or crumpled it onto the ground.

… and Moses fell down swooning…: He fell down dead or unconscious, being shocked by that scene.

… And when he recovered, he said, “Immaculate are You! I turn to You in penitence…”: I repent to You of my request.

… and I am the first of the believers”: I am the first to believe that You cannot be seen.

The above is the most apparent meaning of the text. Yet, there is room for further contemplation.

What is Meant by Seeing

What the common mind would understand from this verse is that it pertains to physical vision through looking with the eyes. It stands to reason—and we shall have no doubt—that physical vision requires a set of physical processes which create an image of the object that is being observed in the visual faculty of the observer. That is how the image would especially by the statement: lan tarānī (You shall never see Me). (Trans.)

1 The author’s point here is to distinguish between naẓar and ruʾyah. Naẓar is the stage when one turns one’s look toward something and searches for it. Ruʾyah is when one’s eyes actually sight the thing. Therefore, ruʾyah (seeing) is subsequent to naẓar (looking). (Trans.)

represent the same shape and color as the object. In short, what we know for sure is that physical vision is realized when there is some physical matter in both the object and the subject.

The Qur’an, however, teaches us very expressly that there is no like or similar for the Almighty God in any aspect whatsoever. God is neither physical, nor has physical properties.1 He is not encompassed by time and space. He is not to be found in any physical direction. There cannot exist any image—whether mentally or externally—that may represent and resemble Him in any way whatsoever. All these are definite Qur’anic principles.

Clearly, such a Being cannot be an object of physical vision, in the way that we see other things. Nor can there be any mental image—whether in this world or in the hereafter—which may correspond to Him and reflect Him. Besides, Moses was a great prophet. He was one of the five Resolute Messengers (ūlū al-ʿazm) who are the chiefs of all prophets. Given his lofty position and grand status, he could not have been ignorant of this. Nor would he entertain the wish that God may empower his eyes to see and observe Him, because we are talking about a Being that is transcendent from motion, direction, space and time. God is free from the

defilement2 of physical matter and its properties. Otherwise, such a desire from Moses would be a frivolous hope, not a serious request.

It is also meaningless to bring up God’s infinite power to justify a physical interpretation. Our visual faculty is a physical property in its essence and nature, which makes it impossible for it to observe a reality

1 “Being physical” and “having physical properties” refer to two planes of existence. Being physical means having a material body with spatiotemporal dimensions, which applies to all beings in the world of nature. Beyond the realm of nature is the imaginal world (ʿālam al-mithāl), where beings do not have a material essence and substance, but they have physical properties. For instance, geometrical shapes do not exist in time and space, but they have shape and form. The author’s point in these discussions is that in order for something to be perceived with the physical eye, it must belong to either of these two realms. If a being is absolutely transcendent, immaterial, and free from all physical properties, then it cannot be an object of eyesight. (Trans.)

2 In metaphysical discussions, words like “defilement” mean existential limitation, and should not be mixed with value judgments, which are fundamentally foreign to metaphysical discourses. (Trans.)

that has absolutely no trace of physical matter and physical properties. No matter how much God strengthens a physical instrument, as long as it is physical in nature, it cannot be applied to something that is beyond matter and material properties. A physical device can only observe something of limited size and boundary.

Given the above points, the vision of God that Moses desired was not physical vision. And as a corollary to this, God’s negative answer was also about a non-physical vision.1 Otherwise, a physical vision of God is out of the question ipso facto. It was neither something to be requested [by a prophet like Moses], nor something to be rejected [in such a context]. There are indeed other verses in the Qur’an which affirm the vision of God and other similar concepts: Some faces will be fresh on that day, looking toward their Lord (75:22-23); The heart did not deny what it saw (53:11);

Whoever expects to encounter Allah [should know that] Allah’s [appointed] time will indeed come (29:5); Is it not sufficient that your Lord is witness to all

things? Look! They are indeed in doubt about the encounter with their Lord! Look! He indeed encompasses all things! (41:53-54); So whoever expects to encounter his Lord—let him act righteously, and not associate anyone with the worship of his Lord (18:110). There are many other verses which can be added to this list. Yet, there are also some verses which deny the vision of God, such as: The sights do not apprehend Him, yet He apprehends the sights (6:103). The current verse is another example of this: He said, “You shall never see Me” (7:143).

So what is intended by verses which affirm the vision of God?

According to some scholars, what is meant by ruʾyah (seeing, vision) is decisive knowledge.2 It is called ruʾyah to emphasize and/or exaggerate the clarity and evidence of that knowledge.

It is true that ruʾyah is a form of decisive knowledge in the Qur’an, but that is not sufficient. We need to dig deeper to find the reality of this decisive knowledge. Not every sure piece of information is called ruʾyah (seeing, vision) or other similar concepts like liqāʾ (meeting, encounter). For

1 In other words, God rejected the same type of vision which Moses demanded. (Trans.)

2 “Decisive” here is a translation of ḍarūrī (necessary, essential, certain). It

means a kind of knowledge that is sure to be true, without even the possibility of a doubt. The author’s examples below help clarify this. (Trans.) instance, we know for sure that there used to be someone called Prophet Abraham, someone called Alexander, and someone called Caesar in the past, even though we have not seen them. We also have decisive knowledge that London, Chicago and Moscow exist, even though we may not

have been there. Yet, we do not use “seeing” to describe our knowledge in these cases, even if we were to emphasize and exaggerate. One may say, “I know about the existence of Abraham, Alexander and the Caesar as though I have seen them” but one would not literally say, “I have seen them.” Similarly, one who has not been to these cities may describe their knowledge of the cities by saying, “I know that London, Chicago and Moscow exist” but one would not say, “I have seen them [before]” or “I see them [now].”

A more patent form of decisive knowledge is our knowledge about self-evident truths, such as: “One is half of two”; “Four is even”; “A relation hinges on two sides.” These are not material or sensory observations

because they are universal statements. They are decisive and necessarily true, but we refer to them as things that we know, not things that we see. It is semantically incorrect to use ruʾyah for such decisive knowledge. This should be clear.

The same can be said about all kinds of acquired knowledge, such as all thoughts and statements that we understand, and all concepts and meanings that we imagine. We call them knowledge, but we do not call them ruʾyah. We say, “I know this,” but we do not say, “I see this.” In such cases, we might use the word “view” (raʾy) in the sense of judgment and position, but not in the sense of observation and experience.

Yet, there remain some forms of knowledge for which we use the term ruʾyah (seeing, vision) without any reservation. Some examples are: “I see that I am myself”; “I see that I want this”; “I see that I don’t want this”; “I see that I like…”; “I see that I hate…”; “I see that I hop…”; “I see that I desire…” In these statements, what is meant is that I find and feel myself directly, without being veiled by anything. I observe in the innermost essence of myself a sense of desire, resentment, love, hate, hope, ambition and so on. It is neither a sensory nor an intellectual observation, but

a feeling that I find within myself.

This should not be mixed with similar statements about others, such as: “I see that you like this” or “I see that you don’t like this.” In these cases,

what is meant is: “I saw you in a certain condition, behaving in a certain way. From that, I deduced that you must like or dislike such-and-such.” This is categorically different from observing one’s own desire, resentment, like and dislike. One finds these things within oneself without any barrier, and without the intermediation of argumentation or deliberation. In

the case of others, however, one arrives at the given conclusion through mental inference and deduction.

It is common to use ruʾyah for one’s personal experience of one’s inner conditions. This is a type of knowledge where the knower observes the very external reality of the known [that is, the object of knowledge].1 This includes one’s knowledge about oneself, one’s inner faculties, one’s personal traits, and one’s psychological conditions. The realization of this kind of knowledge does not depend on any physical condition such as direction, time or place. The reader must reflect on this very carefully.

This sense of observation (ruʾyah) is indeed what is meant in the Qur’anic verses which affirm divine vision. There are some indications and evidence in these verses which clarify this meaning for us. Some examples are:

(1) Is it not sufficient that your Lord is witness (shahīd) to all things? Look! They are indeed in doubt about the encounter with their Lord! Look! He indeed encompasses all things! (41:53-54). The first verse states that God is present with everything, where He is either the witness or witnessed.2 The second verse states that He encompasses all things. These

two qualities—of being a witness over all things and encompassing them all—apply to God not in a physical sense. His presence is not restricted to any particular direction, place or object. Therefore, if He were to be found and observed, He would be found both outside and inside, encompassing not only the person, but also the person’s cognition, observation and

experience. The same applies to the encounter with their Lord [mentioned between the two qualities of witnessing and encompassing all things]. What is meant is not a physical encounter, which occurs only when two

1 This is called presential and immediate knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḥuḍūrī). In the other forms of knowledge, called acquired knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḥuṣūlī), the known is not directly present with the knower, but is available through a mental image of it that corresponds to its external reality. (Trans.)

2 This depends on how the word shahīd is interpreted in the verse. In the Qur’an,

it always means “witness” as a subject, not “witnessed” as an object. (Trans.) objects are physically aligned with one another in the same time and place. (2) The heart did not deny what it saw (53:11). In this verse, “seeing” is ascribed to the heart, which is undoubtedly the rational human soul,1 not the piece of flesh that is on the middle-lefiiside of the chest.

(3) When Our signs are recited to him, he says, “Myths of the ancients!” No indeed! Rather, their hearts have been sullied by what they have been earning (83:14-15). According to these verses, what veils one from God is the rust of disobedience, which one acquires through sins. This defilement obstructs one’s heart—meaning one’s soul and self—from one’s Lord.

Hence, they lose the privilege of observing the divine. This means that if they were to see God, it would have been through their hearts—that is, their soul and self—not through their physical eye.

(4) No indeed! Were you to know with knowledge of certainty, you would surely see hell. Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty

(102:5-7). These verses also affirm some form of seeing that is different from physical sight.

(5) Thus did We show Abraham the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of those who possess certitude (6:75). We discussed this verse previously, and explained that malakūt means the inner orientation of things, as opposed to their visible aspect.2 The above discussion should clarify that there are two types of vision in the Qur’an: (1) sensory vision through the physical eyes; (2) an inner consciousness of oneself without the involvement of sensory or mental instruments. We humans have a certain shuʿūr (consciousness, cognizance, sense, feeling) of our Lord other than our acquired belief through

thinking, argumentation and evidence. Our divine consciousness is a direct experience. It is not veiled by anything. Nor can anything make us distracted and heedless of it, except for our occupation with ourselves and the sins we commit. But even so, that would still be a form of

ghafiah (heedlessness, inadvertence, distraction), which is different from ignorance. It means that one is inadvertent of some reality that is present

2 See volume 13 (1st ed.), pp. 217ffof the English translation. Also, see verses

This is the special type of decisive knowledge that God has affirmed for Himself in the Qur’an, and has called it ruʾyah (seeing, vision) and liqāʾ (meeting, encounter). W hether these terms are used literally or figuratively is not our concern. As we explained above, the circumstantial evidence

Back to the Verse:

When Moses arrived at Our tryst and his Lord spoke to him, he said, “My Lord, show [Yourself] to me, that I may look at You!”…: Moses requested to “see” God, which, as we explained, means a special kind of decisive knowledge about the divine. This request was subsequent to several stages of divine knowledge which God bestowed upon him. God first gave Moses knowledge of Himself through reflecting on His signs. Then He advanced Moses’ knowledge by choosing him as His messenger and speaking to him, which is a form of knowing God through hearing. At that stage, Moses hoped that he could also realize knowledge through seeing, which is the highest stage of decisive knowledge of God. After all, God is the best One to be hoped and trusted.

This is what he requested, not “seeing” in the sense of physical sight with the eyes. A noble prophet like Moses would be far from not knowing that such vision of God is impossible.

As long as one is busy with managing the body and taking care of various needs to survive, one will not realize a state of total severance from everything but God. That will only occur when one is cut offfrom all things, including one’s body and its properties, which amounts to death.

The meaning is: You are never capable of seeing me—in the sense of decisive knowledge—in this world until you encounter Me [after death]. At that point, you will know Me with the kind of decisive knowledge that you desire.

… You shall never (lan) see Me…: The apparent meaning of the negational particle lan is “never,” which indicates everlasting negation. This,

however, need not extend to the hereafter. The decisive knowledge being negated here could be realized at that point, and this does not contradict the usage of lan (never) in the verse, because as long as something does not occur for the duration of this world, it is sufficient for the usage of lan. Some other Qur’anic examples of using lan for everlasting negation only in this world are: Indeed you will never (lan) pierce the earth, nor ever (lan) reach the mountains in height (17:37); Indeed you can never (lan) have patience with me! (18:67).

Even if one insists that the apparent meaning of lan in this verse is total negation in both this world and the hereafter, we could draw on the verse: Never (lan) will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until (ḥattá) you followed their creed (2:120). Here, the apparently everlasting negation lan (never) is qualified with ḥattá (until, unless), which indicates the possibility of an end to it.1 Therefore, we could say that other verses which affirm the vision of God in the hereafter—like Some faces will be fresh on that day, looking toward their Lord (75:22-23)—would similarly qualify the apparent everlasting negation in the current verse.

… You shall never see Me…: The negation here pertains to Moses’

capability and endurance. This interpretation can be confirmed by the next part of the verse: But look at the mountain: if it abides in its place,

The meaning is: My appearance and manifestation to the mountain is similar to My appearance to you. So if this great mountain, with its high degree of endurance, can stay as it is in its place, then you too can hope to endure the appearance and manifestation of your Lord.

… But look at the mountain: if it abides in its place, then you will see Me…: This statement does not prove that divine manifestation is impossible. How could it be impossible when God indeed manifested to the

mountain? Rather it is meant to show and teach Moses that he is incapable of bearing the divine manifestation. If God were to manifest to him, Moses would not abide in its place, which means he would cease to exist, just as it happened to the mountain as it crumbled.

… So when his Lord disclosed Himself to the mountain, He crumbled it…: As we said, this statement shows that divine manifestation is possible. The mountain was crushed and transformed into tiny dust particles, which means that it lost its identity as a mountain. God’s manifestation gave an end to the mountain’s term [of existing as a mountain].

… and Moses fell down swooning…: The context shows that Moses fell down swooning because of the shock and terror of observing that scene. Here we must remind ourselves that Moses was the one who throw the staff, whereby it turned into a manifest python, and swallowed thousands of pythons and snakes. He was the one who split the sea, and drowned thousands and thousands of Pharaoh’s clan in a single moment. He was the one who raised the mountain above the heads of the Israelites as though it were a cloud. He was the one who performed many other miracles. These things were more shocking and extensive than the collapse of the mountain, but he was not terrified by any of them. The crumbling of the mountain was lesser than those events. Moreover, he was apparently immune from any harm, because God crushed the mountain in order to show him something.

We can thus infer that what made him faint was a realization that occurred to him with respect to his request, and the absolute dominance of God which he came so close to witness. Of course, he did not witness it himself, but the mountain did, and that resulted in its total destruction, whereby it could not stay in its place even for the blink of an eye. This interpretation [of the cause of his swooning] can be confirmed by his repentance after his recovery, as we shall see presently.

… And when he recovered, he said, “Immaculate are You! I turn to You in penitence (tubtu, from tawbah)…”: Moses repented and turned to God in penitence because he realized that his request was out of place. God embraced him in His grace to show him that his request is impossible [in this world]. He taught him this lesson experientially through the

destruction of the mountain as He manifested to it.

Moses first glorified God and proclaimed His sanctity with respect to his previous notion that it is possible to see God [in this world]. Then he stated his repentance of what he had done, indicating his hope that God would also return to him [with mercy and forgiveness]. The applicability of tawbah (repentance, penitence) is not restricted to cases of some

sin or disobedience. Rather, it means returning to God after any sense of distance in any way. We discussed this in volume 4 of this book.1 … and I am the first of the believers”: Given the context, what is meant is: “I am the first one among my people to believe that You cannot be seen.” Another possible meaning is: “I am the first believer among my people because of Your guidance and blessing. I believed in You before they did. Therefore, it befits me to repent to you of any intentional or unintentional shortcoming.” However, this meaning is unlikely [given the verse’s context].

(7:144) He said, “O Moses, I have chosen you over (iṣṭafaytuka ʿalá) the people with My messages and My speech. So take what I give you, and be among the grateful.”

Iṣtifāʾ means “choosing (ikhtiyār) what is most refined and pure.” That is why its object, the people, is introduced with the preposition ʿalá (over, on, above).2 It should be noted that My messages are different from My

These meanings and messages could be conveyed to him either through the intermediation of an angel, or directly cast upon his heart. Even if the messages were communicated to Moses through speech, they refer to the meanings that he received as the audience, not to the speech itself.

“Speech” refers to direct communication between God and Moses, without the involvement of an angel. “Speech” is something that unveils what the speaker holds within. What is meant here is not the kind of speech that is common among us humans. We have assigned certain sounds to certain meanings by convention, in order to direct the audience’s mind to our intended meaning. When we wish to convey a meaning to another person, we create certain sound waves in the air, which originate from us and end at the audience. This form of speech requires physicality, while God is free from that. Meanwhile, God’s speech should not be

interpreted as the mere creation of some sound waves and vibrations in the air. That is not sufficient to show that the meaning conveyed by those sounds is in fact what God had intended to convey. One needs something beyond the sounds to uncover God’s intention. This can be compared to when someone creates a knocking or beating sound to convey a meaning. In order to know what the person intends, they must have indicated to us previously, either explicitly or implicitly, that this is indeed what they mean by that sound.

In the Qur’anic accounts of God’s speech with Moses, he never asks God for some indication to ascertain that this is indeed God’s speech, or that this is God’s intended meaning. For instance, when Moses heard the call from the right side of the Mount from the tree, he did not inquire, “Is this from you, my Lord? And is this what you mean?” Instead, he was completely certain about it. This holds about all forms of divine revelation, including those that are not through speech.

This shows decisively that the audience must have a unique connection with what is intended by the speaker of revelation. It is through that

connection that the audience would know the intention behind the speech. the people.” (Trans.)

Otherwise, just because some sound is created by God which has some meaning in a language does not grant the ascription of that meaning to God as His speech. After all, all words that are uttered by all speakers are sounds that trace to God, but they do not count as God’s speech. They are rather attributed to other speakers. Similarly, it may happen that two objects collide with one another, and emit a sound that has a meaning in some language. Yet, we do not consider that to be God’s speech.

In short, God’s speech is when He creates a special connection and link between His audience and the unseen, such that the audience would arrive at His intended meaning through observing something of God’s creation. This could be concomitant with the creation of some sounds in the air or in the ear of the audience, and it could be through other channels. We had “A Talk about the Speech of Allah” previously, and shall add

a few more points in Sūrah al-Shūrá, if God wills.1 Either way, this verse—He said, “O Moses, I have chosen you… (7:144)— is meant to show God’s favor upon Moses. He is also admonished to be content with being chosen by God with His messages and His speech, to be grateful for them, and not to demand more than that.

(7:145) And We wrote for him in the Tablets (al-alwāḥ, from law.) from all things some advice and some elaboration of all things, [and We said], “So hold on to them with power, and bid your people to hold on to the best of [what is in] them. Soon I shall show you the abode of the transgressors.”

Some advice is a descriptive addition for all things.

… and some elaboration (tafṣīlan) of all things…: The conjunction

The effective meaning is: We wrote for Moses in the Tablets—that is, the Torah—a selection of everything. By that, what We mean is that We wrote for him some advice and some elaboration and explanation for everything with respect to religious beliefs and practices, as per the needs of his people.

This verse implies that the Torah did not cover everything that humankind needs in terms of religious teachings and laws. This can also be

deduced from another verse, which says after a mention of the Torah and the Gospel: We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, confirming what was before it of the Book, and encompassing them (5:48). We already had a discussion on this verse.1

… [and We said], “So hold on to them (fa-khudhhā) with power, and bid your people to hold on to the best of [what is in] them…”: The letter fāʾ (so, therefore, then) at the beginning of this part indicates consequence and conclusion. The sentence is added to: And We wrote for him in the Tablets… , which indicates that the entire verse is something that was said to Moses. The implied meaning is: “We said to him, ‘We have written for you in the Tablets from all things some advice, so hold fast to them.’” “Holding on to something with power” is a metaphorical expression for determination and seriousness. If one is seriously determined about something, they will use all their power, lest they lose that thing. Therefore, holding with power is a necessary implication of serious attention and determination. The verse refers to seriousness and determination indirectly through their implication.

… and bid your people to hold on to the best of [what is in] them…: The pronoun “them” apparently refers to all things, including the admonitions and elaborations of rites and laws. “Holding on to the best of something” means choosing, following, and siding with goodness in all affairs.

When one is concerned with what is good in all circumstances, then if they are confronted with good and evil, they would choose the good. And if they face good and better, their love for goodness would lead them to choose the better and give it a higher priority over the good. Therefore,

As we said, they were commanded to adhere to the path of goodness in all affairs, and to follow guidance and truth. If one transgresses from this path, God will divert them from the straight path of guidance to pursue evil and error, as we shall see more elaborately in the next verse. The end of such individuals will be eternal loss and destruction. Therefore, the next verse—Soon I shall turn away from My signs (7:146)—is an interpretation (or almost an interpretation) of this phrase: Soon I shall show you the abode of the transgressors (7:145). Here are some other suggested meanings for the abode of the transgressors: (1) It refers to hell, with a tone of warning and threat.

(2) It refers to the houses of Pharaoh and his people in Egypt.

(3) It refers to the houses of the tribes ʿĀd and Thamūd.

(4) It refers to the houses of the Amalekites and other tribes in the Levant. God will make the Children of Israel enter those towns to see their end.

(5) It means that a transgressing lot will come at you and rule over you.

(7:146) “Soon I shall turn away from My signs those who are unjustly proud in the earth, and [even] though they should see every sign, they will not believe in it, and if they see the way of rectitude they will not take it as [their] way, and if they see the way of error they will take it as [their] way. That is because they deny Our signs and are oblivious to them.” All forms of takabbur (arrogance, pride) are unjustified, much like all baghy (aggression, injustice).1 Yet, the verse qualifies pride in the earth with

being unjust. Such qualifications in the Qur’an are descriptive (tawḍīḥī), not restrictive (iḥtirāzī). W hat is meant is to criticize and condemn the action. It means that pride and aggression are reprehensible because they are unjustified.

Some exegetes have suggested that unjustly is added as a restrictive qualification to rule out rightful forms of pride, such as showing arrogance against the enemies of God, and against those who are proud themselves. Therefore, unjustly serves to clarify that what is meant here is only condemnable pride.

The problem with this interpretation is that the verse does not mention “pride” unconditionally in its general sense, but it is about “pride in

the earth,” which means seeking ascendancy over the servants of God, enslaving them, and domineering over them. Such forms of pride are necessarily unjust.

… and [even] though they should see every sign, they will not believe in it…: The conjunction “and” shows that this is another attribute of those who are unjustly proud in the earth. That is, they insist on disbelief and denial [of the truth].

… and if they see the way of rectitude they will not take it as [their] way, and if they see the way of error they will take it as [their] way…: This is a similar addition to their previous descriptions. The verse explicitly mentions both the negative and positive aspects of their behavior with respect to their paths in order to show their attitude. They are very careful and highly sensitive to oppose the path of growth, and to follow the way of error. Their behavior is such that one cannot give them the benefit of the doubt, and there remains no possibility that perhaps they were ignorant or mistaken.

… That is because they deny Our signs and are oblivious to them”: This sentence justifies why they have developed the above mentioned vices. It means: “They behave the way they do because of denying Our signs and being heedless of them.” This sentence could also be a justification for the

(7:147) Those who deny Our signs and the encounter of the Hereafter, their works have failed (ḥabiṭat, from ḥabṭ). Shall they be requited (yujzawna, from jazā.) except for what they used to do?

The verse’s meaning should be clear. We can infer two points from this verse: First, the result of an act is the act itself. We discussed this repeatedly in our previous discussions. Second, ḥabṭ (cancellation, failure, annulment) is also part of one’s actions which will be given to the person as their result. If one’s action is a failure, then that failure will be the person’s result. Ḥabṭ is only applicable to actions which have some aspect of

good. For instance, suppose someone who has both good acts and evil acts. If their good acts are cancelled, it means that they will receive painful results for their evil deeds, but will not receive any reward for their good deeds. This amounts to an evil requital.

Another possible interpretation is that jazāʾ (result, requital, payment) in this verse is about good reward in particular. Therefore, Shall they be requited except for what they used to do? is a way of saying that they will not be rewarded for anything, because they will have no good deeds with them, since all their good deeds have failed. The Qur’an says: We shall attend to the works they have done and then turn them into scattered dust

(25:23). The reason why jazāʾ here means reward in particular is that it pertains to the previous part of the verse about their works, which have failed, and the failure (ḥabṭ) of acts is only applicable to righteous deeds. Some exegetes have said: There is no punishment for one who does not fulfill an obligatory act as long as they do not do anything sinful contrary to that, because this verse states that punishment is only for what

one commits: Shall they be requited except for what they used to do? Response: This argument is fiawed because, as we explained above, jazāʾ (result, requital, payment) in this verse means reward. The meaning is: They will have no reward in the hereafter because they did not bring

Moreover, it is almost known by necessity from the Qur’an that not performing God’s commands is a sufficient condition for one’s punishment, regardless of whether the person commits sinful acts contrary to

(7:148) The people of Moses took up in his absence a calf (ʿijlan) [cast] from their ornaments (ḥiliyyihim)—a body that gave out a lowing sound (khuwār). Did they not regard that it did not speak to them, nor did it guide them to any way? They took it up [for worship] and they were wrongdoers.

Ḥulī means “adornments and embellishments” such as gold and silver. It is the plural of ḥaly, just as thudī is the plural of thady (breast, mamma). ʿIjl means “calf.” Khuwār (lowing, mooing) is the specific sound of cattle. … a body that gave out a lowing sound…: This expression is an additional description for the calf. It indicates that it was not a living calf, but

only emitted a lowing sound like that of cattle.

This verse and the following verses discuss the story of the Children of Israel worshiping the calf. That was when Moses had gone to the tryst of his Lord, and they felt his absence was too long. Thus the Samaritan (al-Sāmirī) deceived them, took their ornaments, and molded a golden calf that gave a lowing sound. He told them that this was their god and Moses’ god. They prostrated themselves before it and adopted it as their god. The story is presented more elaborately in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā.1 The account given in these verses does not cover the details there, which confirms the view that Sūrah Ṭā-Hā was revealed before Sūrah al-Aʿrāf. Either way, the verse can be interpreted as follows:

The people of Moses took up in his absence a calf [cast] from their ornaments…: They did so between the time that Moses had gone to the

1 See verses 20:83-97. (Trans.)

tryst of his Lord and his return. The subsequent verses talk about his angry return.

… a body that gave out a lowing sound: The calf that they adopted as god and worshiped was such.

… Did they not regard that it did not speak to them, nor did it guide them to any way?…: God chides them for not paying attention to a clear and evident criterion of reason at first sight. If the calf is really a god, then

it should speak to them and guide them to the right path.

The verse mentions only two attributes of the calf which were incongruous with its divinity: it did not speak, and did not guide them to any

path. There are many other attributes that also contravene divinity, such as being physical, being manufactured, being limited, being temporal, being spatial, having a shape, and so on. The two qualities mentioned in the verse—not speaking and not guiding—are among the first and foremost attributes of a god. If one is to adopt something as a god, then the

servant must know what pleases that god, and how to approach it. This can only be known by some form of speech and communication from the god, which would guide the servant to the proper way of its worship. However, it was clear to the calf-worshipers that their god neither speaks to them, nor guides them to any way.

Moreover, they saw and knew from before that God spoke to Moses and guided him; and through him He also spoke to the Israelites and guided them. Yet, when the Samaritan made the calf for them, they said: This is your god and the god of Moses, which he has forgotten (20:88). So if the calf were really the god described by the Samaritan [that is, the God of Moses], then it should have spoke to them and guided them.

Overall, it must have been more than evident to their intellects that the calf is not their God, only if they were to think. That is why the verse adds: They took it up [for worship] and they were wrongdoers. It is as though one had asked: “So why did they take up the calf despite its case being so clear?” And the verse explains: They took it up [for worship] and they were wrongdoers.

(7:149) But when they became remorseful and realized they had gone astray, they said, “Should our Lord have no mercy on us, and forgive us, we will be surely among the losers.”

The first part of the verse literally says, “But when it fell in their hands.” Majmaʿ al-bayān explains:

The implied pronoun “it” in “It fell in their hands” (suqiṭa fīaydīhim) refers to balāʾ (calamity, affliction, misfortune). “Falling in hands” means that they found it right there with them, as though it were in their hands. This expression is used in cases of remorse and regret, when the person realizes something that was hidden from them. Both suqiṭa and usqiṭa are used, although suqiṭa is more eloquent.1 According to some, the meaning is: “That which is harmful to them was cast in their lap.”

The extensive books of tafsīr have offered many interpretations for this expression, but most—if not all—of them are contrived. The most plausible one is what we quoted from Majmaʿ al-bayān, which has been quoted from other exegetes anonymously.2 We can also deduce the meaning of this expression from the verse’s context, as follows.

But when they became remorseful and realized they had gone astray…: That is, when they noticed what they had done, pondered over it a second time, and saw that they had gone astray. As we can see, this expression implies awareness about something that they had neglected, and insight about something that they had ignored. It is as though they did something and presented it to the person for whom they had worked, but he returned their work to themselves and threw it back at them. Then they picked it up; “it fell in their hands.” Upon seeing it from near, they realized that what they had thought was wrong, and they had disregarded what they should not have disregarded. They found out that they missed something that caused their work to be ruined. At any rate, this phrase [“it fell in their hands”] is used as a proverb or figure of speech.

… Should our Lord have no mercy on us, and forgive us, we will be surely among the losers: This is an expression of their remorse and regret over what they had done and what they missed. What is mentioned in this

The explanation here is that knowledge has certain effects and implications, while observation has other effects and implications. Anger is when our defensive faculty is excited and aroused to either defend or avenge. However, one does not express this by merely knowing about the case. There emerged a very heated debate around this topic from the early years of Islam, especially during the times of Imams al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq, up to the time of Imam al-Riḍā. The Muʿtazilites denied the physical vision of God outright, while the Ashʿarites affirmed its possibility in the hereafter. Both groups quoted this verse to support their view. There was also

another group which affirmed it in both this world and the hereafter. This debate continued to persist and did not subside, except with the swords of Āl Ayyūb, who exterminated the Muʿtazilites and finished them off. Apparently that is what gave an end to this dispute.

The Muʿtazilites’ position can be summarized as follows: they relied on the statement, You shall never see Me (7:143), as well as other scriptural evidence and rational proofs which deny physical vision. With respect to the verses and narrations that suggest physical vision, they offered other interpretations [different from their apparent meanings].

The Ashʿarites’ position can be summarized as follows: they relied on the comparison made in the verse: But look at the mountain: if it abides in its place, then you will see Me (7:143), as well as other verses and some narrations which suggest the possibility of physical vision in the hereafter. As with the contrary evidence and arguments, they offered other interpretations [different from their apparent meanings], just as they do in all

theological discussions. Some of them argued that there is no basis for restricting physical vision to physical bodies. Rather, it is possible to see non-material things with the physical eye. One of their arguments was: (a) Physical vision is applicable to substance and accident both.1 (b) The only common denominator between substance and accident is that they are both categories of mawjūd (existent, being) in its unconditional sense. (c) Hence, any existent can be observed with the eye, even if it is free from having a body or physical properties.

The implausibility of these two positions—and other similar views and arguments—is more than clear in our time and age. In fact, their invalidity can be compared to the validity of self-evident statements (badihiyyāt). At any rate, it is not our purpose to discuss how each group has defended itself and criticized the other side. Interested readers should refer to the books of theology and lengthy Qur’anic commentaries of each group. We clarified two points in our exposition of the verse:

(i) It is impossible to observe God through physical vision, whether in this world or the next. This includes our current eyesight, as well as any modified and transformed vision that involves material instruments in order to perceive physical properties such as size, form, color and light. This impossibility is supported by rational arguments, as well as the Qur’anic verses and narrations which negate divine vision. As with the verses and narrations which apparently affirm divine vision, what they mean is the realization of a special form of decisive knowledge of God, which will occur in the hereafter. There are clear indications and circumstantial evidence in these scriptural sources which support this interpretation. This type of decisive knowledge—which is called vision (ruʾyah)—is

different from the kind of knowledge that one acquires through rational argumentations and mental processes.

God is Always Known to Everyone

But how is it that God is known to every knower [of anything]? To explain and understand this, we must bear in mind that any created being relies on God in every aspect. It is not possible to find anything that is independent of God in any way whatsoever, whether in the external world, or in the mind. The existence of any created thing is like a relation or copula that cannot be found independently from the other side—that is, the Source on which it relies—in any way. Furthermore, when we have a knowledge of anything, that thing appears in our cognitive receptacle, as we explained above. However, no created being can be found in any mode of existence unless it is supported by God and relies on Him. Otherwise, it would be an independent entity from the Absolute [not something created]. Hence, no knower can comprehend its known object unless it first

Now, the knower is also created, which means that it depends on God in all its aspects, including its knowledge, because the entire existence of the knower is supported by God. If the knower could have its own knowledge independently of God, then it would no longer be a created being.

This means that the knower also relies on God in order to be a knower, just as the known relies on God in order to be known. Dissecting the Hadith

Let us discuss the above noble tradition [number 15] part by part: “Whoever thinks that they can know God through a screen (ḥijāb), a form (ṣūrah) or an analogy (mithāl), is a polytheist.” There are a few possible interpretations for the three terms in this statement: (1) Apparently

ḥijāb (screen, veil, intermediary) means anything that is assumed to separate Him from His knower. Ṣūrah (form) means a mental image that

corresponds to the physical qualities of the external object, such as light, color and size. Mithāl (analogy, symbol) means an intellectual concept beyond the visible. (2) Ṣūrah means a physical form, while mithāl means an imaginary form [which is conceived and constructed mentally]. (3) Ṣūrah means a bare concept that is grasped and conceived (taṣawwur), while mithāl means a statement that is predicated and confirmed (taṣdīq). Either way, all intellectual and mental knowledge would be included under these categories. There are very many narrations which deny the possibility of comprehending God through intellectual and mental knowledge.

Such knowledge of God [through a screen, form or analogy] would be polytheism because it implies that there is something out there that is neither the Creator nor created. At the same time, it serves as an intermediary for knowing God, which means that it is the same as Him in a

The mental image partakes of the meaning and quiddity of the known object in the external world, but does not share its existence. This makes the known object be composed of quiddity and existence.1

(Trans.) “So if someone thinks that they can know God through something else, how can they be a monotheist?” Such a person effectively holds that there is some composition in the divine essence, and there is some counterpart and partner for God in existence.

“Anyone who knows God, would only know Him through Himself.”

That is, one can only know God through knowing the divine essence, not through some intermediary.

“If someone does not know Him through Himself, then they do not know Him, but they know something else.” The next sentence explains why: “There is nothing to intervene between the Creator and the created.” That is, there is nothing else besides them to connect them to one another. “God has created all things not from any [other] thing.” There is no other thing to serve as a link between them, connecting the Creator to the created, and vice versa. For instance, what connects an artisan to their artifact is the mental image in the artisan’s mind, and the raw material that they use.

“He is called by some names, but He is other than His names.” This is an answer to an implied question (called a prolepsis). One might object here: “We know God through His names which describe His beauty and majesty.” So the Imam anticipates and answers that possible objection by saying that the very act of using names to denote God necessitates some distinction and difference between Him and those names. Otherwise, knowing Him through His names would be the same as knowing Him through Himself, not through anything else. The Imam then reiterates this by saying that names to the divine essence are like adjectives to a noun, “The noun is not the same as the adjective [which describes it].” One might raise another objection here: “We believe in a God that we do not know. It is not possible for us to know Him by Himself. We can only know Him through His signs. This can be called a knowledge of God only in a figurative sense.” Thus the Imam answers: “If one thinks that they believe in something without knowing it, they have missed the knowledge [of God].” One who makes the above claim does not really know what they are saying, because they certainly comprehend something, and there is no point trying to deny that.

“No creature can comprehend anything except through God.” Thus, every knower [of anything] knows God. It is not possible to know anything through God without knowing Him first.

“And the knowledge of God cannot be achieved except through God.” There is no other way to realize this.

“God is empty of His creation; and His creation is empty of Him.” That is, there is no common relation in some middle ground between the Creator and the created.

Based on this narration, any being that has any share of knowledge, intelligence and consciousness, knows God by necessity. The only thing is that many knowers are ignorant of their knowledge, and confused in this regard. One who knows God, would know Him by Himself, and would realize that: (i) they know God; (ii) they know everything else through Him. There are also other narrations which express some of the points mentioned in this hadith.

The reader should know that the narrations in this regard from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt are numerous indeed. There is no need to quote them all here. In addition, we did not open a philosophical chapter on this subject of vision because most of the narrations discussed above are philosophical in nature. That is why there was no need for a separate philosophical discourse.
